approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would create a new expert body to advise the government on tackling long-term disadvantage and improving economic inclusion.
The committee, with up to 13 part-time members including economists and community advocates, would report annually before each federal budget.
The social services minister and treasurer would choose the members together, and the committee's operation would be reviewed within five years.
Establishes the Economic Inclusion Advisory Committee as a statutory body.
Requires the committee to provide annual advice on income support adequacy and barriers to participation.
Allows the minister and treasurer to jointly direct the committee to examine specific issues.
Requires an independent review of the committee's operation within five years.
Australians facing disadvantage, the government, and experts in economics, academia, business, unions and community advocacy.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2023-11-28.83.2) to agree with the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a second time. This means they can now discuss it in more detail. ### What does this bill do? According to the [bill homepage](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r7094), the bill: > *Establishes the Economic Inclusion Advisory Committee to provide advice related to the Commonwealth Government’s policies, programs and responsibilities for enhancing economic inclusion and participation.*

The majority voted against an amendment introduced by Clark MP [Andrew Wilkie](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/clark/andrew_wilkie) (Independent), which means it failed. ### What do these amendments do? Mr Wilkie explained that: > *These amendments insert poverty reduction into each of the listed matters for consideration by the committee as they formulate any report.
